issues: 'Do Not Track was never made mandatory' is too absolute. On 24 August 2023 the Landgericht Berlin (16 O 420/19, vzbv v. LinkedIn; not final when announced) held that under the GDPR 'A DNT signal represents a valid objection' and barred LinkedIn from telling users it ignores DNT. No statute made DNT binding. The narrower claim holds, and the ruling is now noted in the correction.

'the Attorney General fined Sephora $1.2 million in 2022 partly for ignoring it' presents allegations as fact. It was a settlement 'resolving allegations', and the AG 'alleged' that Sephora 'failed to process user requests to opt out of sale via user-enabled global privacy controls'. The correction is reworded to say this.
The Colorado claim (honour universal opt-out mechanisms from 1 July 2024) had no source on this record. It is true, and a Colorado AG source is added.

The DNT quote did not itself say the working group stopped. The next sentence on the same page does: 'The working group has therefore decided to conclude its work'. The quote is extended to include it. The title and date (W3C Working Group Note 17 January 2019) are correct.
The OAG CCPA quote ('Under law, it must be honored by covered businesses ...') is verbatim and refers to the GPC. The verdict MISLEADING is fair.

fieldFixes.correction: Do Not Track never became a binding standard: the W3C working group concluded its work in January 2019 because there had not been sufficient deployment or planned support, and no privacy statute made honouring it an explicit duty (its one notable legal success came late, when a Berlin district court held in August 2023, in a judgment not final when announced, that under the GDPR a DNT signal is a valid objection). GPC differs in having explicit legal force in some places: California's CCPA regulations require covered businesses to treat it as a valid opt-out of sale or sharing, and in 2022 Sephora agreed to pay $1.2 million to settle the Attorney General's allegations, which included failing to process GPC opt-outs; Colorado has required controllers to honour recognised universal opt-out mechanisms, GPC first among them, since 1 July 2024. Where no such law applies, it remains a request.

sourceFixes.quote: Since its last publication as a Candidate Recommendation, there has not been sufficient deployment of these extensions (as defined) to justify further advancement, nor have there been indications of planned support among user agents, third parties, and the ecosystem at large. The working group has therefore decided to conclude its work and republish the final product as this Note, with any future addendums to be published separately.

fieldFixes.legalForce: Binding in California as a valid opt-out under the CCPA regulations (2020; now 11 CCR §7025), in Colorado as a recognised universal opt-out mechanism from 1 July 2024, and in a growing number of other US states whose privacy laws require controllers to honour opt-out preference signals (Connecticut, for example, from 1 January 2025). In California it featured in the Attorney General's 2022 settlement with Sephora. Elsewhere a request.
